pe131_richard_white_middle_ground_prefac.title: Richard White, 'Preface to the twentieth anniversary edition', The Middle Ground (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2011), from p. xi.
pe131_richard_white_middle_ground_prefac.citation: Richard White, 'Preface to the twentieth anniversary edition', in The Middle Ground: Indians, Empires, and Republics in the Great Lakes Region, 1650–1815, twentieth anniversary edition (Cambridge University Press, 2011), from p. xi.

verification.note: Google Books search-within snippets (volume fHLfiOZVzmMC). Copyright page: 'First published 1991 Twentieth anniversary edition 2011'; contents: preface p. xi, introduction p. xxv (the preface's last page was not seen). Quoted: the book 'has jumped disciplines, moving into literary criticism, anthropology, archaeology' (p. xi); he cites Philip Deloria, 'What Is the Middle Ground, Anyway?', William and Mary Quarterly 63 (January 2006) (p. xii); 'I always thought that the middle ground as a process was present in other places and other times: I did not, however, think that every time you find this process at work you would find the construction of a coherent space that is the equivalent of pays d'en haut' (p. xiii); Hämäläinen's Comanche Empire, where 'no middle ground emerges' (p. xv); Havard, Empire et métissages, read as seeing the middle ground 'only as a tool of French manipulation of Indians' (p. xvi); the middle ground 'did not involve the achievement of a widespread mutual understanding and appreciation between Europeans and Indian peoples. People did not come together to love one another' (p. xxi); Merrell, Into the American Woods (1999) (pp. xx–xxi). Snippets only. Fix pass 2026-10-13 (sol-review-1.131): a re-try to reach page images (Google Books page view) returned 403 on 2026-10-13, so the wording remains snippet-witnessed; atlas text paraphrases White's own framing passages and labels the rest as snippets. Classification: Merrell (1999) is an in-period critique known here only through this later response; Havard (2003) and Deloria (2006) are later critiques. Addendum 2026-10-27: Revision 1.201: a Portuguese translation of this preface, 'Prefácio à edição de vigésimo aniversário', Topoi 22, no. 46 (2021): 281–297, is cited by Fontella (2022), who quotes it at pp. 283 and 287; the translation was not located on SciELO and is unread. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.1)

pe131_richard_white_middle_ground_prefac.scope_note: Later reading (2011): the author's answer to critics. Not evidence for any edge.

pe135_cook_atlantic_1993.title: Ramsay Cook, “The New History of Atlantic Canada,” Acadiensis 23, no. 1 (Autumn 1993): 146–152 (review essay on E. R. Forbes and D. A. Muise, eds., The Atlantic Provinces in Confederation, 1993).
pe135_cook_atlantic_1993.citation: Ramsay Cook, “The New History of Atlantic Canada,” Acadiensis 23:1 (Autumn 1993): 146–152.

verification.note: Read in full in the UNB Libraries Acadiensis PDF (OJS article 11967). The citation line printed on p. 146 gives Acadiensis XXIII, 1 (Autumn, 1993), pp. 146–152; signed RAMSAY COOK. Quoted: 'one of the sweet ironies in the arid debate between “nationalists” and “limited identitarians” on historiography is that neither side appears to recognize that class, ethnicity and gender describe what groups of Canadians have in common, while “nationalism” most often provokes divisions — “regionalism”!'; Canadians 'have, in fact, been growing more alike, at least in aspiration if not in reality' (p. 146); Histoire du Québec contemporain makes Quebec 'what Michel Brunet always denied: a “normal” society' (p. 147); the Atlantic Provinces as 'the scene of fragmentation and conflict' (p. 152). His note on being introduced as a Torontonian who subscribed to Acadiensis 'from the beginning' (p. 147) is the passage Buckner 2000 (p. 8) cites.

pe135_cook_atlantic_1993.scope_note: Cook's in-period position between the 'nationalists' and the 'limited identitarians'.

pe135_cook_burden_1977.title: Ramsay Cook, “The Burden of Regionalism,” Acadiensis 7, no. 1 (Autumn 1977): 110–115 (review essay).
pe135_cook_burden_1977.citation: Ramsay Cook, “The Burden of Regionalism,” Acadiensis 7:1 (Autumn 1977): 110–115. Review of Mildred Schwartz, Politics and Territory (1974); David Cameron, Nationalism, Self-Determination and the Quebec Question (1974); and David Bercuson, ed., Canada and the Burden of Unity (1977).

verification.note: Read in full in the UNB Libraries Acadiensis PDF (OJS article 11456; the OJS record misspells the author 'Ramsey Cook'; the review is signed RAMSAY COOK, p. 115; running heads give pp. 111–115, and the first page is 110 per the OJS record). Volume and issue follow Buckner 2000 n. 15 (VII, 1); Buckner dates it Autumn 1974, but the OJS record and the 1977 books reviewed, Bercuson 1977 and Alexander's Canadian Forum letter of September 1977 (n. 1), date it 1977. Quoted: 'the tendency to see regionalism as a virtue of Canadian life rather than an obstacle to Canadian unity'; the Laurentian view hardly acceptable 'as “national”' in the Fraser, Red or Restigouche valleys, 'a point made long ago by W. L. Morton'; 'And the other nationalist themes fare little better' (p. 110); Bercuson's contributors assume 'that Canadian history is best understood from a regional perspective' (p. 112); no one 'attempts to define the term' (p. 114); the regional approach 'has both strengths and weaknesses. The whole may not be greater than the parts, but it is at least the sum of them' (p. 115).

pe135_cook_burden_1977.scope_note: Cook's own in-period review essay on regional history and the Laurentian view.

pe135_cook_unmasked_1983.title: Ramsay Cook, “Regionalism Unmasked,” Acadiensis 13, no. 1 (Autumn 1983): 137–142 (review of L. D. McCann, ed., Heartland and Hinterland: A Geography of Canada, 1982).

verification.note: Read in full in the UNB Libraries Acadiensis PDF (OJS article 12212; OJS author 'Ramsey Cook'; signed RAMSAY COOK, p. 142; running heads pp. 137–142). Volume and issue follow Buckner 2000 n. 15 (XIII, 1, Autumn 1983). The first words of p. 137 ('SINCE THE 19ÔOS') are garbled in the text layer, so the decade is not quoted. Quoted: the 'national' approach 'has come under a destructive barrage of criticism'; Berger's book 'a lengthy epitaph on the headstone of the national school's grave'; Morton's 'Clio in Canada' 'made explicit what had long been implicit in the Innis-Creighton laurentian thesis' (p. 137); Wynn's chapter 'the finest section of the book' (p. 138); 'I have begun to doubt seriously the existence of the phenomena we have for so long called regions'; 'So why not call a region what it really is — a province' (p. 140); 'as a tool of analysis, “regionalism” is a concept whose time has gone'; 'Stripped of its rhetoric ... a legitimate preoccupation with ... class, sex, family, ethnicity' (p. 141). Buckner 2000 (p. 8) quotes the key sentence as 'whose time is gone'; the page reads 'has gone'.

pe135_cook_unmasked_1983.scope_note: Cook's own in-period critique of region as a unit of analysis.

iha_fontella_white_2022.title: Leandro Goya Fontella, 'Entrevista escrita com o Prof. Richard White (Universidade de Stanford) por Leandro Goya Fontella', História (São Paulo) 41 (2022), e2022054.
iha_fontella_white_2022.citation: Leandro Goya Fontella, 'Entrevista escrita com o Prof. Richard White (Universidade de Stanford) por Leandro Goya Fontella', História (São Paulo) 41 (2022), e2022054.

verification.note: Read in full (open access, 27 pp.). The answers were received by email on 30 April 2021 in English; the published text is Fontella's own Portuguese translation ('tradução livre', p. 1 note), so White's answers may only be paraphrased or quoted in Portuguese, never given as English quotations. Pages are the article's own 'N DE 27' folios. Passages: p. 10, the New Indian History 'parece bastante primitiva agora' and the agency argument 'poderia ir longe demais, disfarçando as enormes forças que muitas vezes matavam muitos deles e destruíam suas sociedades'; p. 10, 'quanto mais Antropologia eu lia, mais crítico eu me tornava do híbrido: Etnohistória'; p. 15, 'estou cada vez mais desconfiado do upstreaming'; p. 16, upstreaming assumes a belief or practice 'contém um significado inato que não muda'; p. 15, a middle ground needs 'um frágil equilíbrio de poder'. Fontella's p. 6 summary of the 2006 WMQ forum is a named reader's account. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-older-scholarship.md §1.1)

hr28_wiebe_white2017.title: Richard White distinguishes his Gilded Age interpretation from Wiebe’s (2017).
hr28_wiebe_white2017.citation: Alex Shashkevich, “Stanford historian reexamines United States’ Reconstruction, Gilded Age in new book,” Stanford News/Department of History,25October2017; interview answers by Richard White on The Republic for Which It Stands.

verification.note: Fresh actual institutional primary interview full body read. White’s own answer identifies Hofstadter and Wiebe, then argues strong interventionist government without administrative capacity fostered corruption; the interviewer/byline and answer speaker remain separate. This is White’s stated criticism, not an unqualified fact that Wiebe’s work lacks all recognition of state action. The full2017book unread. raw/white2017.html/.txt.
